'''Hirono:''' {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Ben Cayetano]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Linda Lingle]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsHI}} The '''2002 Hawaii gubernatorial election''' was held on November 5, 2002. Incumbent Democratic Governor [[Ben Cayetano]] was term-limited and therefore could not run for re-election. Former [[Mayor of Maui|Maui Mayor]] [[Linda Lingle]], who had narrowly lost the [[1998 Hawaii gubernatorial election|1998 election]], was nominated once again by the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republicans]] while [[Lieutenant Governor of Hawaii|Lieutenant Governor]] [[Mazie Hirono]] earned the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] nomination in a tight race. Lingle and Hirono duked it out in a hard-fought campaign, with Hirono's campaign crippled by allegations of corruption within the [[Hawaii Democratic Party]] and many voters desiring a change.{{cite news |last1=Broder |first1=John M. |title=THE 2002 CAMPAIGN: THE DEMOCRATS; Hawaii Democrats Reeling After Scandals and a Death |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2002/10/19/us/2002-campaign-democrats-hawaii-democrats-reeling-after-scandals-death.html |access-date=21 August 2019 |agency=The New York Times |date=19 October 2002}} The influence of migrants from the mainland as well as the decrease in party loyalty of ethnic groups led more voters towards Lingle.{{Cite web |date=November 7, 2002 |title=THE 2002 ELECTIONS: HAWAII; In the 50th State, the End of the Democrats’ 40-Year Streak |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2002/11/07/us/2002-elections-hawaii-50th-state-end-democrats-40-year-streak.html |access-date=November 25, 2024 |website=The New York Times}} Ultimately Lingle defeated Hirono in a close election, making her the first [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor of Hawaii elected since [[1959 Hawaii gubernatorial election|1959]] and the state's first-ever female governor. She was the first white person to be elected governor of the state since 1970. Lingle and Hirono faced off again in Hawaii's [[2012 United States Senate election in Hawaii|2012 U.S. Senate election]]; Hirono won that race and thus became the first female U.S. senator in Hawaii history. As of 2026, 2002 is the last Hawaii gubernatorial election where the winner did not win every county. ==Democratic primary== ===Candidates=== *[[Mazie Hirono]], [[Lieutenant Governor of Hawaii]] *[[Ed Case]], Majority Leader of the [[Hawaii House of Representatives]] *[[D. G. Anderson]], 1982 and 1986 [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] nominee for [[Governor of Hawaii]], former [[Hawaii State Senate|Hawaii state senator]] *George Nitta Jr., radio personality *Art P. Reyes, perennial candidate *Joe Fernandez, school bus driver Mazie Hirono was Hawai'i's lieutenant governor from 1994 to 2002 under Ben Cayetano. Cayetano had loss democratic support due to links to a bad economy and bad relationships with labor groups. Hirono had to separate her image from Cayetano. She originally was not in the race for governor, but the race for mayor. Mayor Jeremy Harris was highly expected to win the Democratic gubernatorial primary but didn't run. Hirono then switched to the gubernatorial race, but with a late start she didn't have much time to campaign and raise money.{{Cite web |last=Blair |first=Chad |date=2011-10-19 |title=When Mazie Met Linda ... and Ed |url=https://www.civilbeat.org/2011/10/when-mazie-met-linda-and-ed/ |access-date=2024-12-02 |website=Honolulu Civil Beat |language=en}} Ed Case was focused on statewide campaigns to win the primary. He was a fresh face in the election. However, he didn't have full support of Native Hawaiians due to a bill he introduced that would combine the Office of Hawaiian Affairs and the Department of Hawaiian Home Lands. Andy D.G. Anderson had run for governor before. He was a Republican turned Democrat but also a Native Hawaiian. He effectively took points away from both Hirono and Case. ===Results=== Hirono beat Case by less than 2% of the votes. However, the Case campaign was ruled a success due to the number of voters he was able to take from a known Democratic face.{{Election box begin no change | title = Democratic primary results{{cite web|title=2002 Primary election results| url=https://files.hawaii.gov/elections/files/results/2002/primary/histatewide.pdf}} }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = Mazie Hirono | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 76,709 | percentage = 41.24 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = Ed Case | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 74,096 | percentage = 39.84 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = D. Reyes | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 568 | percentage = 0.31 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = Joe Fernandez | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 491 | percentage = 0.26 }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 185,995 | percentage = 100.00 }} {{Election box end}} ==Republican primary== ===Candidates=== *[[Linda Lingle]], former [[Mayor of Maui]], [[Hawaii gubernatorial election, 1998|1998]] Republican nominee for [[Governor of Hawaii]] *[[John Carroll (Hawaii politician)|John Carroll]], former [[Hawaii House of Representatives|Hawaii state representative]] *Crystal Young John Carroll was running on experience from military and business; he believed Hawaii's citizens needed a governor with both military and political experience.{{Cite news |date=2002-01-20 |title=Article clipped from Honolulu Star-Advertiser |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/honolulu-star-advertiser/41328949/ |access-date=2024-12-02 |work=Honolulu Star-Advertiser |pages=38}} Carroll attempted to use Lingle's non Republican views against her. His campaign appealed to Lingle's opponents in the GOP as Lingle was not a typical Republican with her support for abortion and opposition of the death penalty.{{Cite web |last=Blair |first=Chad |date=2022-10-09 |title=Chad Blair: How Did Republican Linda Lingle Become Governor Of Hawaii? |url=https://www.civilbeat.org/2022/10/chad-blair-how-did-republican-linda-lingle-become-governor-of-hawaii/ |access-date=2024-12-02 |website=Honolulu Civil Beat |language=en}} A campaign brochure of Carroll states “John Carroll stands with the social conservatives that Lingle has alienated.” Carroll's campaign was unsuccessful due to lack of funding and inability to win over Native Hawaiians and their activists due to suing the [[Office of Hawaiian Affairs]] for being “racially discriminatory”.{{Cite web |title=It's Hirono vs. Lingle {{!}} The Honolulu Advertiser {{!}} Hawaii's Newspaper |url=http://the.honoluluadvertiser.com/article/2002/Sep/22/ln/ln01a.html |access-date=2024-12-02 |website=the.honoluluadvertiser.com}} ===Results=== {{Election box begin no change | title = Republican primary results }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = Linda Lingle | party = Republican Party (United States) | votes = 70,808 | percentage = 89.77 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = John Carroll | party = Republican Party (United States) | votes = 7,616 | percentage = 9.66 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = Crystal Young | party = Republican Party (United States) | votes = 454 | percentage = 0.58 }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 78,878 | percentage = 100.00 }} {{Election box end}} ==General election== ===Campaign=== Lingle was critical of the way that Hirono had handled education and economic issues as lieutenant governor; in a TV spot premiered by the Lingle campaign in September, the Republican noted that "Reading scores are now among the worst in the nation. We rank last in jobs creation and first in poverty increase" and argued that Hirono bore part of the blame.{{cite web |title=Lingle Unveils New Political Ad Blasting Mazie Hirono's Record |url=https://www.hawaiinewsnow.com/story/949960/lingle-unveils-new-political-ad-blasting-mazie-hironos-record/ |website=Hawaii News Now |publisher=Gray Television |access-date=June 14, 2021 |date=September 26, 2002}} Hirono responded that low reading scores could be attributed to the fact that many Hawaiian students — such as Hirono, herself an immigrant from Japan — were learning English as a second language. She also pointed to legislation which she had supported to "improve teacher quality" and boost test scores, and commented that "I'd like to know what Linda has done" to further the cause. Native Hawaiians’ vote became a deciding factor. Ben Cayetano stopped Public Land Trust (PLT) funds from being transferred to the Office of Hawaiian Affairs (OHA). Many programs that supported Native Hawaiians could no longer operate without these funds. The OHA held a gubernatorial debate where PLT funds were the main focus. Hirono didn't make any commitments but Lingle promised to restart PLT funds. Lingle's stance on Native Hawaiian affairs was a strong part of her campaign.{{Cite web |last=Wong |first=Sterling |date=2018-08-02 |title=History shows power of the Hawaiian vote
